chief_complaint: sudden generalized tonic-clonic seizures, severe headache, and visual scotomas at 36 weeks gestation
hpi_details: 29F G1P0 at 36 weeks gestation brought to ED by ambulance after husband witnessed her experience a 2-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. For the past 2 days, patient complained of severe, unrelenting frontal headache, flashing lights/blind spots in her vision, and rapid swelling of her hands and face. Still post-ictal and confused upon arrival.
ideas: husband terrified she and the baby will die from stroke or brain hemorrhage
concerns: husband wants immediate emergency delivery and medicine to stop any more seizures
expectations: patient currently post-ictal with blood pressure spiking dangerously high
pmh: No prior chronic medical history. Prenatal course notable for borderline blood pressures starting at 34 weeks without proteinuria at last check

investigation_events.title: Emergency maternal and fetal assessment
investigation_events.availability_message: STAT maternal laboratory and fetal-monitoring results are now available. Magnesium, severe-hypertension treatment, and delivery preparation must not be delayed.

results.value: Baseline 150 bpm with minimal variability and recurrent late decelerations after the seizure

clinical_knowledge.topic: Eclampsia (seizure secondary to severe preeclampsia) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Eclampsia (seizure secondary to severe preeclampsia) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes STAT obstetric emergency with magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, acute blood pressure control, and stabilization for urgent delivery, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden generalized tonic-clonic seizures, severe headache, and visual scotomas at 36 weeks gestation

Key HPI features: 29F G1P0 at 36 weeks gestation brought to ED by ambulance after husband witnessed her experience a 2-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. For the past 2 days, patient complained of severe, unrelenting frontal headache, flashing lights/blind spots in her vision, and rapid swelling of her hands and face. Still post-ictal and confused upon arrival.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 118, BP 188/116 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96% post-ictal. 4+ pitting edema of lower extremities and facial puffiness. Deep tendon reflexes 4+ bilaterally with 3 beats of clonus at ankles. Continuous fetal heart rate monitoring reveals baseline 150 bpm with minimal variability and late decelerations post-seizure. Labs: Protein/Creatinine ratio 4.8 g/g (marked proteinuria), Platelets 95,000 /uL, AST 142 U/L, ALT 156 U/L, Uric acid 8.4 mg/dL.
Relevant background/PMH: No prior chronic medical history. Prenatal course notable for borderline blood pressures starting at 34 weeks without proteinuria at last check
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Eclampsia (seizure secondary to severe preeclampsia).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Severe preeclampsia without seizure without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Generalized tonic-clonic seizure.
management_principles: STAT obstetric emergency requiring seizure prophylaxis, acute blood pressure control, and stabilization for urgent delivery

Initiate Magnesium Sulfate IV bolus (4 grams over 20 minutes) followed by continuous infusion (2 grams/hour) for seizure prophylaxis and neuroprotection (monitor patellar reflexes, respiratory rate >12, and urine output >30 mL/hr; have Calcium Gluconate readily available for toxicity)
Lower acute severe hypertension using IV Labetalol (20-40 mg IV bolus) or IV Hydralazine (5-10 mg IV bolus) targeting systolic BP 140-150 / diastolic 90-100 mmHg to prevent maternal stroke
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: sudden generalized tonic-clonic seizures, severe headache, and visual scotomas at 36 weeks gestation

29F G1P0 at 36 weeks gestation brought to ED by ambulance after husband witnessed her experience a 2-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. For the past 2 days, patient complained of severe, unrelenting frontal headache, flashing lights/blind spots in her vision, and rapid swelling of her hands and face. Still post-ictal and confused upon arrival.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 118, BP 188/116 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96% post-ictal. 4+ pitting edema of lower extremities and facial puffiness. Deep tendon reflexes 4+ bilaterally with 3 beats of clonus at ankles. Continuous fetal heart rate monitoring reveals baseline 150 bpm with minimal variability and late decelerations post-seizure. Labs: Protein/Creatinine ratio 4.8 g/g (marked proteinuria), Platelets 95,000 /uL, AST 142 U/L, ALT 156 U/L, Uric acid 8.4 mg/dL.
reference_soap.assessment: Eclampsia (Seizure secondary to Severe Preeclampsia at 36 weeks gestation) with secondary fetal distress.
reference_soap.plan: STAT obstetric emergency: 1. Initiate Magnesium Sulfate IV bolus (4 grams over 20 minutes) followed by continuous infusion (2 grams/hour) for seizure prophylaxis and neuroprotection (monitor patellar reflexes, respiratory rate >12, and urine output >30 mL/hr; have Calcium Gluconate readily available for toxicity). 2. Lower acute severe hypertension using IV Labetalol (20-40 mg IV bolus) or IV Hydralazine (5-10 mg IV bolus) targeting systolic BP 140-150 / diastolic 90-100 mmHg to prevent maternal stroke. 3. Stabilize maternal condition and proceed to urgent/emergent delivery (Cesarean section if fetal distress/late decelerations persist post-maternal stabilization).

learning_objectives: Recognize the clinical progression of preeclampsia with severe features (headache, visual changes, hyperreflexia, clonus) to Eclampsia (seizure)
Administer correct IV Magnesium Sulfate loading and maintenance dosages and monitor toxicity signs (loss of patellar reflexes, respiratory depression, oliguria)
Understand the therapeutic threshold and selection of rapid-acting antihypertensives (IV Labetalol, IV Hydralazine, oral Nifedipine) for maternal hypertensive emergencies (BP > 160/110)
Explain that delivery of the fetus and placenta is the only definitive cure for preeclampsia/eclampsia, while maternal stabilization precedes surgical delivery during acute seizures

teaching.one_liner: 36-week primigravida with new-onset seizure, headache, visual scotomas, and facial/hand swelling on a background of rising blood pressure.

must_ask.objective: Confirm the seizure characteristics and duration
must_ask.say: Can you describe what happened during the seizure — how long did it last?

must_ask.objective: Elicit premonitory symptoms of severe preeclampsia
must_ask.say: Did you have a headache, blurred vision, or flashing lights before this happened?
Have you noticed sudden swelling in your hands, face, or legs?

must_ask.objective: Screen for epigastric pain (impending eclampsia sign)
must_ask.say: Have you had any pain under your ribs or in your upper stomach?
Has your blood pressure been high at any of your prenatal visits?

history.answer: I am 36 weeks pregnant, and my husband said I had a violent seizure in bed about an hour ago. My head is pounding severely and I still feel so confused and exhausted.
My husband said my whole body suddenly went completely stiff and then started shaking violently all over. He told me my eyes rolled up and stayed open while I shook.
He told the paramedics the shaking lasted about two full minutes. It has only happened once, but I have been sleepy and confused ever since.

Right before it happened, my frontal headache became unbearable and I saw flickering bright spots and dark patches in front of my eyes. I did not smell anything strange or feel anything rising from my stomach.
My husband told me the jerking did not begin in just one hand or my face—it seized my entire body all at once, without my head turning to either side.
My tongue feels sore and my husband noticed some blood where I bit the side of it, and I also lost bladder control during the seizure.
I still feel heavily dazed, exhausted, and confused about how I got to the hospital, and my body aches all over. My frontal headache is still pounding, but both my arms and legs can move.
I was lying in bed when the shaking started, so I did not fall onto the floor or strike my head or shoulders.
I have never had a seizure, blackout, or convulsion before in my life. I have never experienced staring spells or morning muscle twitches either.
I have not had any fever, chills, or neck stiffness. It is just this unrelenting, terrible headache across my forehead.
The severe frontal headache started two days ago and steadily worsened without any relief. I have not had personality changes or arm or leg weakness leading up to this.
I have not been sleep-deprived or under severe unusual stress, and I have not been around strobe lights or missed any medications.
I do not drink alcohol, especially during my pregnancy, and I have never used any recreational or illicit drugs.
I do not have diabetes and do not take insulin. I have been eating regular meals and have not had any nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
I have never suffered a head injury, stroke, brain aneurysm, or brain infection like meningitis.
No one in my family has ever had epilepsy, recurrent seizures, or febrile seizures during childhood.
I teach high school, so I do not work around dangerous machinery or high places. I normally drive to school, but my husband drove before the ambulance arrived.
Over the past two days, my face became very puffy and my hands and feet swelled up so fast that my wedding ring became stuck.
I have had a dull ache in the upper right part of my stomach right under my ribs since yesterday, but no sharp cramps or vomiting.
history.topic: Epigastric or right upper quadrant pain

history.answer: At my routine prenatal visit two weeks ago, my doctor noted my blood pressure was borderline high around 135 over 85, but my urine was clear at that time.
The baby was moving normally earlier this morning, but since the seizure I have barely felt any kicks, which terrifies me.
My husband is horrified that I might have had a stroke or a brain bleed, and we are terrified our baby is dying.
We need emergency medicine right away to stop any more seizures and save our baby.
I have never had high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart trouble, or any chronic medical illnesses before this pregnancy.
I have never had surgery, and I have never been hospitalized before this pregnancy.
I only take daily prenatal vitamins prescribed by my obstetrician. I have not taken any over-the-counter painkillers or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I work as a high school English teacher and live in a house with my husband.
My mother has mild high blood pressure, but no one in my family has a history of preeclampsia, stroke, or seizures.
This is my first pregnancy, and I am currently 36 weeks pregnant calculated from my last normal menstrual period.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 188/116 mmHg, heart rate 118 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air.
Somnolent, post-ictal young pregnant woman lying in bed with marked facial puffiness and swollen hands.
Lethargic and oriented to person only, confused regarding time and place, responding slowly to verbal prompts.
Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light at 3 mm bilaterally without papilledema on fundoscopic view.
Shallow laceration with dried blood on the left lateral border of the tongue; no airway obstruction.
Supple neck with no resistance to passive flexion; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are negative.
Tachycardic regular rhythm without murmurs, third heart sound, or friction rubs.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with normal respiratory excursion and no crackles or wheezing.
Gravid uterus consistent with third-trimester pregnancy; mild tenderness on deep palpation over the right upper quadrant without rebound or guarding.
Marked 4+ pitting edema bilaterally up to the mid-calves and tight non-pitting puffiness of both hands.
Moves all four extremities spontaneously with symmetric 5/5 motor power and no focal limb weakness.
Bilateral 4+ patellar and biceps deep tendon reflexes with 3 beats of sustained ankle clonus.
